items.front: Two most abundant gases in dry air by volume?
items.back: Nitrogen ~78% and oxygen ~21%; then argon 0.93%, CO₂ 0.03%.
items.examPoint: Atmospheric composition — N₂ 78%, O₂ 21%, CO₂, ozone, water vapour, aerosols
items.source: NCERT Geography

items.front: Which layer has all weather; which holds the ozone layer?
items.back: Troposphere = all weather (lapse rate 6.5°C/km); stratosphere = ozone layer (15–30 km), ideal for flying.
items.source: NCERT Geography

items.front: Earth's heat budget: reflected vs absorbed units of 100?
items.back: 35 reflected (albedo), 65 absorbed (14 atmosphere + 51 surface); re-radiated as long-wave — balance = 65.
items.examPoint: Insolation, albedo, heat budget & greenhouse effect
items.source: NCERT Geography

items.front: Global pressure belts and their two named ones?
items.back: Equatorial low (doldrums), subtropical high (Horse latitudes ~30°), subpolar low, polar high; shift with the Sun.
items.source: NCERT Geography

items.front: Coriolis force — direction and where zero/max?
items.back: Deflects winds right in N, left in S hemisphere; zero at equator, maximum at poles.
items.examPoint: Planetary winds — trades, westerlies, polar easterlies; jet streams
items.source: NCERT Geography

items.front: Local winds: Loo, Chinook, Mistral, Foehn — where?
items.back: Loo = N. India (hot); Chinook = Rockies (warm 'snow-eater'); Foehn = leeward Alps; Mistral = Rhone valley (cold).
items.examPoint: Local winds — loo, chinook, foehn, mistral, sirocco
items.source: NCERT Geography

items.front: Conditions needed to form a tropical cyclone?
items.back: SST > 27°C, Coriolis force (none at equator), low vertical wind shear, pre-existing low, upper-level divergence.
items.examPoint: Tropical vs temperate (extratropical) cyclones — formation & structure
items.source: NCERT Geography

items.front: Tropical vs temperate cyclone — fronts and movement?
items.back: Temperate: has fronts, moves W→E, over land/sea. Tropical: no fronts, moves E→W, only over warm seas.
items.examPoint: Tropical vs temperate (extratropical) cyclones — formation & structure
items.source: NCERT Geography

items.front: Cold vs warm front weather?
items.back: Cold front = steep, cumulonimbus, brief violent rain then drop. Warm front = gentle, cirrus→nimbostratus, prolonged steady rain.
items.source: NCERT Geography

items.front: Who names north-Indian-Ocean cyclones, and Montha's contributor?
items.back: IMD (New Delhi RSMC) under WMO/ESCAP panel of 13; the name 'Montha' was given by Thailand.
items.source: IMD

items.front: AP cyclone chronology: Hudhud, Titli, Michaung, Montha — where & when?
items.back: Hudhud 2014 Vizag; Titli 2018 N.AP (Srikakulam); Michaung 2023 Bapatla; Montha 2025 Narasapuram.
items.examPoint: AP cyclone chronology — Hudhud (2014, Visakhapatnam), Titli (2018, N. AP), Michaung (2023, Bapatla), Montha (2025, Narasapuram)
items.source: IMD

items.front: El Niño, La Niña and positive IOD effect on Indian monsoon?
items.back: El Niño → weaker monsoon; La Niña → good monsoon; positive IOD → favours rain, can offset El Niño.
items.examPoint: ENSO (El Niño/La Niña) & Indian Ocean Dipole
items.source: IMD

items.front: SW vs NE monsoon — period and where NE rains?
items.back: SW June–Sept (Kerala ~1 June, most of India); NE (retreating) Oct–Dec brings rain to coastal AP & Tamil Nadu.
items.examPoint: Indian monsoon mechanism — SW/NE, ITCZ, burst & break
items.source: NCERT Geography

items.front: Sendai Framework & India's DM setup basics?
items.back: Sendai 2015–2030 (after Hyogo): 4 priorities, 7 targets. NDMA under DM Act 2005, chaired by PM; NDRF responds.
items.examPoint: Disaster management institutions — DM Act 2005, NDMA, NDRF, NIDM, APSDMA
items.source: UNDRR / DM Act 2005
